slides.name: 1 · Full picture
slides.notes:
0–5 min. Welcome back. Week 1 introduced why we visualise and the What–Why–How framework. Today connects data types to visual choices. Ask: what made one chart from last week memorable? Plan: foundations 10 min, integrity 25 min, data and channels 25 min, colour 15 min, critique and questions 15 min. Allow a short pause around the data-abstraction divider. Cover artwork is illustrative, not empirical evidence.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 2 · This week

params.text:
Worksheets: Canvas by 12:00 on the Friday after the lab.
Reading: Munzner, Chapter 2, What: Data Abstraction.
Start during the lab. Ask for help early and leave time to review.

slides.notes:
Keep housekeeping under one minute. Distinguish worksheet deadlines from assessment deadlines. Chapter 2 is the assigned reading in the supplied Week 2 materials. Chapters 5 and 6 support today’s channel and design discussion.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 3 · What you will practise

params.text:
Distinguish categorical, ordinal and quantitative attributes.
Match a visual channel to a comparison task.
Explain how a chart can distort its data.
Critique a design using perceptual evidence.

slides.notes:
Read these as promises you intend to keep. The fourth is the one that changes how they argue in the lab: 'I don't like it' becomes 'that channel cannot carry that data'.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 4 · Reading the data

params.text:
Chapter 2: What: Data Abstraction
What are the items, attributes and links?
Which attributes identify items? Which record values?
Does the dataset contain spatial structure?

slides.notes:
Munzner, Visualization Analysis and Design (2014), Chapter 2. Example: a table of stations has station ID as a key, daily hires as a value and coordinates as spatial information. Domain meaning matters, but abstraction helps us reuse design knowledge across domains.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 5 · Data, encoding and perception

params.text:
Data: the values and relationships to communicate.
Encoding: the marks and channels that represent them.
Perception: how a viewer interprets those marks.

slides.notes:
Visual communication uses visual elements to convey information. In this lesson the aim is understanding, insight and decisions. Ask students for a failure at each stage. Inaccurate data, an unsuitable channel and an unclear legend can each undermine a chart.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 6 · The greatest value of a picture is when it forces us to notice what we never expected to see.

params.text: The greatest value of a picture is when it forces us to notice what we never expected to see.

slides.notes:
Pause on Tukey’s quotation. Ask for an example of a chart that revealed something surprising. Quotation supplied in the original Week 2 lecture. Portrait is the one from the original Week 2 deck, cropped away from the baked-in quote text so the words are the theme’s, not the picture’s.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 7 · Framed picture

params.text: Brazilian cotton textiles · production, factories, capital, imports and tax, on one sheet

slides.notes:
No lecture text on this one — let them look. Ask what they can find in thirty seconds, then ask which encodings are doing the work. Small multiples, a ring for regional share, paired bars for imports. Then the useful question: which of these choices would you keep, and which would you now defend differently after today? Framed 3:2 rather than full bleed because a dense sheet has to be seen whole — a caption over the artwork would cover the very thing they are reading.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

args.caption: Tecidos de Algodão, 1927
args.credit: Brazilian cotton textiles · production, factories, capital, imports and tax, on one sheet

feedback.prompt: What can you discover in this graphic in 30 seconds?

slides.name: 8 · Design criteria

params.text:
Effectiveness: does the viewer reach an accurate understanding?
Efficiency: how much effort does that take?
Aesthetics: does the presentation invite attention?

slides.notes:
Discuss the trade-offs: simplicity and completeness, novelty and familiarity, beauty and clarity. A familiar chart may serve a time-pressured audience better. Ask which goal matters most for a hospital dashboard versus an exhibition graphic.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 9 · What a good chart has to do

params.text: What a good chart has to do

Effectiveness — it conveys the information you intended, accurately.
Efficiency — it costs the reader as little effort as possible.
Aesthetics — it looks considered, and belongs where it is published.

slides.notes:
The three primary goals from the supplied Week 2 deck. Say that they are ranked: an efficient, handsome chart of the wrong quantity is still a failure. Efficiency is the one students under-weight, because they read their own chart fluently — they already know what it says.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 10 · The design brief

params.text:
What should the audience understand?
Who will read the chart?
What decision or question will it support?
Will they see a slide, report or interactive display?

slides.notes:
The third is the one that changes designs. 'What decision gets made from this' turns a chart of everything into a chart of the thing that matters. Ask the room for their AE1 answer to it.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 11 · Three trade-offs you cannot avoid

params.text:
Simplicity vs completeness — cut until the message is clear; the next cut takes the evidence.
Novelty vs familiarity — a new idiom buys attention and spends comprehension.
Beauty vs clarity — when the two disagree, the reader’s answer decides.

slides.notes:
Trade-offs, not rules: each one is a dial that the design brief sets, which is why the brief comes first. Ask the room which dial their own coursework chart has set wrongly, and what it was bought with.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 12 · Section · Graphical integrity

params.text: Tufte's question: does the picture say what the numbers say?

slides.notes:
The spine of the lecture. Everything from here to the rules of thumb is one argument — the graphic is a measurement, and a measurement can be wrong.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 13 · Tufte’s six principles of graphical integrity

params.text: Tufte’s six principles of graphical integrity

Proportion — size on the page matches the quantity.
Labelling — label thoroughly; explain on the graphic itself.
Data, not design — show data variation, not design variation.
Standardised units — for money over time, deflate before plotting.
No spare dimensions — never more dimensions than the data has.
Context — do not quote data out of context.

slides.notes:
Tufte, The Visual Display of Quantitative Information. The rows are shortened to fit; his wording is: (1) the representation of numbers, as physically measured on the surface of the graphic itself, should be directly proportional to the numerical quantities represented; (2) clear, detailed and thorough labelling should be used to defeat graphical distortion and ambiguity — write out explanations of the data on the graphic itself, label important events in the data; (3) show data variation, not design variation; (4) in time-series displays of money, deflated and standardised units of monetary measurement are nearly always better than nominal units; (5) the number of information-carrying (variable) dimensions depicted should not exceed the number of dimensions in the data; (6) graphics must not quote data out of context.

The supplied Week 2 deck announces six and prints five, because the last two are run together in one paragraph; they are separated here. Principles 1 and 5 are the ones the lie factor and the 3D examples test later in this section. Principle 4 is the one nobody applies until they plot a decade of prices.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials (01_Lecture_IPDV_2_2, slide 10).

slides.name: 14 · The polling challenge

params.text:
At A, is candidate 5 ahead of 3?
From A to B, who improves more: 2 or 4?
Who gains across all three polls?

slides.notes:
3 min. These are illustrative election polls from the supplied lecture, not a real election dataset. First allow 30 seconds of silent reading, then 60 seconds in pairs. Ask students to state both an answer and confidence. Keep candidates identified by number, not colour alone. Do not reveal the next slide until the class has attempted each comparison.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 15 · Aligned bars reveal the differences

params.text:
At A, candidate 5 leads candidate 3.
Candidate 2 rises from A to B. Candidate 4 falls.
Candidate 1 gains across A, B and C.

slides.notes:
2 min. Same source data and candidate order as the preceding pies. The scanned figure’s values are approximate, so do not present exact measurements as raw data. Ask which question became easier. Common baselines and lengths support comparisons better than separated angles. The rightmost poll shows candidate 1 ahead and candidate 5 behind.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 16 · Graphical integrity

params.text:
Keep visual size proportional to the quantity.
Label the measure, units and relevant events.
Keep encodings and scales consistent.
For money over time, consider inflation and standard units.
Avoid adding visual dimensions that exaggerate values.
Keep the relevant context.

slides.notes:
Tufte, The Visual Display of Quantitative Information, Chapter 2. These paraphrase all six principles in the supplied lecture, including its final context principle. Consistent scales matter when panels invite direct comparison. Explain that nominal money can still answer a nominal-money question, so label what the measure means.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 17 · The lie factor

params.text: Relative change in the graphic ÷ relative change in the data

slides.notes:
Use relative changes with the same reference value. Example: data rises from 100 to 110, a 10% increase. A graphic rising from 10 mm to 30 mm shows a 200% increase. Lie factor = 200/10 = 20. A value near 1 preserves the relative effect. The supplied historical fuel-economy example uses 783/53 ≈ 14.8. A zero baseline matters for bar length. A line chart need not start at zero, but its scale and context must remain clear.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 18 · Check · Graphical integrity · 1

params.text: Values rise from 100 to 110 (10%). Their displayed bar lengths rise from 10 mm to 30 mm (200%). What is the lie factor?

slides.notes:
2 min. Invite an individual answer, then ask for the reason before showing the explanation. Use a show of hands if students are not connected. Revisit the example if answers are split.

Lie factor = relative effect in graphic / relative effect in data = 200% / 10% = 20. Use percentage changes from the same reference, not the ratio of final lengths.

slides.name: 20 · Common sources of distortion

params.text:
Truncated bar baselines exaggerate length differences.
Aspect ratio changes how steep a trend appears.
Selected date ranges can hide the wider pattern.
3D perspective can obscure or enlarge marks.
Different panel scales can defeat comparison.

slides.notes:
Ask students to distinguish a deceptive choice from an appropriate choice for a stated task. Line charts can use a restricted axis with clear labels. For bars, the quantitative channel is length from a baseline.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 21 · Cumulative and quarterly sales
slides.notes:
Use the before/after reveal. The supplied Apple graphic shows cumulative iPhone sales. The Quartz comparison adds quarterly sales. Ask: can total sales rise while quarterly sales fall? Yes: positive sales add to the total even when the quarterly rate falls. Cumulative totals can plateau, so avoid saying they always rise. These are historical source images, not current sales figures.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 22 · Useful ink

params.text:
Keep marks that explain the data.
Remove decoration that competes with the comparison.
Retain useful labels, reference lines and context.

slides.notes:
Tufte’s data-ink principle is a design heuristic. A bare chart is not automatically better. Ask which elements in the source examples help interpretation and which obstruct it. Distinguish memorability from numerical accuracy.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 23 · Rules of thumb, with judgement

params.text:
Keep categories distinguishable. There is no universal 7±2 limit.
Use labels or another channel alongside colour.
For exploration: overview, zoom and filter, then details.
Start with a familiar chart suited to the task.

slides.notes:
Miller (1956) discusses absolute judgement and immediate memory, not a universal chart-category limit: https://psychclassics.yorku.ca/Miller/ . Visible legends, channel choice and task change what people can distinguish. Shneiderman (1996), The Eyes Have It, proposes overview first, zoom and filter, details on demand. Treat these as starting points to test with users.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 24 · Section · What: data abstraction

params.text: Describe the data without mentioning what it is about.

slides.notes:
Munzner Chapter 2 proper. The discipline is to stop saying 'it's sales data' and start saying 'it's a table of items with two quantitative and one categorical attribute'.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 25 · Four dataset structures

params.text:
Table: items described by attributes.
Network: nodes connected by links.
Field: values sampled over space.
Geometry: spatial shapes and positions.

slides.notes:
Munzner, Chapter 2. Ask pairs to classify station hire records, routes between stations, air temperature across London and borough boundaries. Answers: table, network, field, geometry. One project may combine them. Fields need not be continuous in every mathematical treatment, but continuous phenomena sampled across space are the familiar example here.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 26 · Attribute types

params.data:
Type	Order?	Meaningful operations	Example
Nominal	No	Same or different	Station name
Ordinal	Yes	Earlier, later, higher	Low / medium / high
Interval	Yes	Differences	Temperature in °C
Ratio	Yes	Differences and ratios	Number of hires

slides.notes:
Nominal means categorical with no inherent ordering. Ordinal labels have an order but no guaranteed equal spacing. Interval and ratio are both quantitative. 20°C is 10°C warmer than 10°C, but not twice as hot on an absolute scale. 20 hires is twice 10 hires. Numeric identifiers remain nominal. Source: supplied Week 2 lecture and Munzner Chapter 2.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 27 · Check · Attribute types · 1

params.text: T-shirt sizes; S, M, L, XL. What kind of attribute is that?
Categorical — the labels are just names
Ordinal — ordered, but the gaps are not measurable
Quantitative interval — ordered with equal gaps, no true zero
Quantitative ratio — ordered with equal gaps and a true zero

slides.notes:
2 min. Invite an individual answer, then ask for the reason before showing the explanation. Use a show of hands if students are not connected. Revisit the example if answers are split.

There is a real order — M is bigger than S — but L minus M is not a number. That is exactly ordinal: order without arithmetic. Encode it with a sequential ramp or position, never with unordered hues.
slides.warn: An answer runs past two lines at the standard size. Shorten it, so every answer fits its button.

slides.name: 29 · Categories need distinct identities

params.text:
Hue, shape and grouping can distinguish categories.
Position and length can show each category’s count.
Pies suit simple part-to-whole questions with few slices.

slides.notes:
The category and its count are different attributes. In a bar chart, the label identifies a category while bar length encodes a quantitative count. Prefer bars when accurate comparisons matter. A small number of pie slices is a practical guideline, not a fixed scientific threshold.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 30 · Ordered attributes need ordered channels

params.text:
Position can communicate rank.
A sequential lightness scale communicates low to high.
Likert responses retain their response order.
Unordered hues alone do not show a sequence.

slides.notes:
S, M, L and XL are ordered but do not imply equal differences. Similarly, agreement levels have order but not automatically equal intervals. Ask students to choose between a rainbow and a sequential heatmap. Explain that sequential schemes may use multiple hues if lightness and perceived ordering remain clear.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 31 · Marks and channels

params.text:
Marks: points, lines and areas.
Channels: position, length, hue, shape and other properties.
A scatterplot uses points and encodes two values by position.

slides.notes:
Ask students to name the mark and channels in the polling bars. Marks are areas (rectangles), length represents support and position identifies a candidate. Source: supplied lecture figure and Munzner Chapter 5. https://www.cs.ubc.ca/~tmm/courses/journ15/slides/journ1.pdf
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 32 · Magnitude and identity

params.text: Daily hires on a common scale
Station type as a distinct symbol

slides.notes:
Hue distinguishes identities but has no inherent numerical order. Position can encode identity through grouping as well as magnitude through an ordered scale. Select a channel for the task, not merely the attribute name.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 33 · Bertin’s visual variables

params.text:
Selective: can one group stand out?
Associative: can marks form a group?
Ordered: can we see a sequence?
Quantitative: can we judge relative amounts?

slides.notes:
Use the source matrix to compare channels. Bertin’s taxonomy provides a conceptual vocabulary. Its classifications are not a universal performance guarantee: task, display and how a variable is implemented matter. Source: supplied lecture’s Bertin figure.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 34 · Accuracy depends on the channel

params.text:
Aligned position usually supports precise comparison.
Angle and area make close comparisons harder.
Choose according to the task and test with readers.

slides.notes:
The supplied Cairo figure summarises graphical-perception research. It is an ordinal hierarchy, not numerical accuracy scores. Cleveland and McGill (1984), Graphical Perception, JASA 79(387). Relate it to the pie/bar experiment. Rankings depend on the task and display. No chart type is universally best.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 35 · Check · Marks and channels · 1

params.text: You need people to compare quantities as accurately as possible. Which channel should carry the number?
Area — bubbles scale naturally with the value
Colour hue — it is the easiest to tell apart
Angle — pie slices are familiar to everyone

slides.notes:
2 min. Invite an individual answer, then ask for the reason before showing the explanation. Use a show of hands if students are not connected. Revisit the example if answers are split.

Cleveland and McGill ranked position along a common scale first for accuracy. Area is well down the list, and hue is an identity channel — it says which, not how much.

slides.name: 37 · Section · Colour and luminance

params.text: Colour communicates order, identity and contrast.

slides.notes:
Week 4 is a whole lecture on colour. Today is the working minimum: pick the right scheme, know that luminance is relative, and design so colour is never load-bearing on its own.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 38 · Colour schemes express structure

params.text:
Sequential: ordered low to high.
Diverging: departures from a meaningful midpoint.
Categorical: distinct groups without an order.

slides.notes:
Ask for a scheme for daily hires (sequential), change relative to zero (diverging) and station operator (categorical). A sequential scheme may use more than one hue. Source and palette guidance: https://colorbrewer2.org/learnmore/schemes.html . Source image supplied in Week 2 lecture.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 39 · Check · Colour schemes · 1

params.text: You are mapping profit and loss by region, where zero matters. Which colour scheme?
Sequential — one hue, light to dark
Diverging — two hues away from a neutral middle
Categorical — a distinct hue per region
Rainbow — the full spectrum covers the range

slides.notes:
2 min. Invite an individual answer, then ask for the reason before showing the explanation. Use a show of hands if students are not connected. Revisit the example if answers are split.

A meaningful midpoint is the signature of diverging data. Sequential would hide the sign change, categorical would deny the order, and rainbow invents boundaries the data does not have.

slides.name: 41 · What colours do you see?

params.text:
Look at the right-hand photograph before discussing.
Compare your answer with someone nearby.
What might your visual system assume about the lighting?

slides.notes:
3 min. Poll first, then invite explanations. There is no wrong perception to score. Differences in assumed illumination help account for differences in appearance. Witzel et al. (2017): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28146253/ . Use the same projected image for the discussion. Avoid reducing the illusion to a simple brightness rule.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

feedback.prompt: What colours do you see in the dress?

slides.name: 42 · Context changes colour appearance

params.text:
The surrounding image influences perceived lightness.
Illumination assumptions influence perceived colour.
Legends and direct labels provide reference points.

slides.notes:
Distinguish luminance (a physical measure) from perceived lightness. Luminance contrast helps reveal structure, but avoid the blanket claim that the eye is always more sensitive to luminance than hue. The supplied image illustrates warm/cool illumination interpretations of the dress. Ask how a map surround might change a viewer’s judgement.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 43 · Identical colours, different surrounds

params.text:
Compare the central squares.
Their surrounds change their appearance.
Avoid relying on a shade alone for exact values.

slides.notes:
Source: simultaneous-contrast figure in the supplied lecture. Ask for a prediction before revealing the explanation. The central patches are intended to match in the source demonstration. Projection and ambient light may alter the strength of the effect.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 44 · Colour needs a second cue

params.text:
Pair colour with labels, position, shape or pattern.
Check contrast at projection size.
Test with colour-vision simulators and real readers.

slides.notes:
The source lecture gives prevalence estimates of 8% and 0.5%. These depend on population and condition, so do not estimate the number of affected students in this room from those figures. The practical design requirement stands without a prevalence claim. A simulator is a useful check, not proof of accessibility.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 45 · A chart critique checklist

params.text: Labels, contrast and cues beyond colour

slides.notes:
Use this checklist in the pair activity. Accept multiple defensible changes, but require a mechanism: which perceptual problem does the change address?
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 46 · Your redesign proposal

params.text:
Pairs, 3 minutes: choose one comparison.
Sketch a better visual encoding.
Explain your choice and one limitation.

slides.notes: 5 min including discussion. Deliberately revisit the opening exercise to assess transfer. A bar chart is reasonable for candidate comparison; a line chart can help track change over A, B and C. Require a stated task, labels and a justification. Do not invent sampling uncertainty absent from the source. Ask what metadata would be needed to assess whether a change is meaningful.

feedback.prompt: What would you change, and why would it help?

slides.name: 47 · Check · Critique, not recall · 1

params.text: A classmate says 'you must never truncate a y-axis; Tufte says so.' What is the strongest reply?
They are right; a truncated axis is always a lie
They are wrong; axes are a matter of taste
It depends on the mark: a bar encodes length so its baseline carries meaning, a line encodes position so it need not start at zero
It only matters if the chart is going to be published

slides.notes:
2 min. Final check: ask students to reason from the channel instead of recalling a universal rule. Discuss the explanation, then invite a remaining question.

Bars encode quantity through length from a baseline. Line charts encode positions and trends, so a clearly labelled restricted range can be appropriate. Always consider the question and whether the scale exaggerates the interpretation.

slides.notes:
